blocks.prompt: The Lizard Who Borrows the Sun
blocks.text: A lizard cannot make its own heat. It has to borrow heat from the sun. In the morning a lizard is slow and cold. It climbs onto a rock and lies flat in the sunshine. Its dark back soaks up the warmth. Soon the lizard is warm, and now it can run and hunt. When it gets too hot, the lizard moves into the shade. All day long it slides from sun to shade and back again. A lizard does not need much food. The sun does most of the work.

blocks.prompt: The Tail That Comes Off on Purpose
blocks.text: Grab a lizard by the tail and you may end up holding only the tail. This is not an accident. Many lizards have weak spots built into the bones of their tails. When something clamps down, the lizard tightens a ring of muscle and the tail snaps off at one of those spots. Special valves squeeze the blood vessels shut, so the lizard barely bleeds. The loose tail keeps twitching on the ground for minutes. A hawk or a cat watches the twitching, and while it watches, the lizard is already gone. Scientists call this autotomy, which means self cutting. A new tail does grow back, but it is never quite the same. The first tail had bones inside. The new one has a rod of rubbery cartilage instead. It is shorter, often a different color, and it cannot break off again the way the first one did. Losing a tail costs the lizard, too. The tail stores fat, and a lizard without one may move slower and win fewer fights until the new tail arrives.

notes: A gecko can hang from glass by one toe

blocks.prompt: The Lizard That Walks on Glass
blocks.text: A gecko can walk up a pane of glass and hang there by one toe. For a long time nobody could explain it. The obvious answers all failed. Geckos have no glue on their feet, and their toes leave no sticky residue behind. They do not use suction, because a gecko sticks perfectly well in a vacuum chamber where there is no air to push. They are not using tiny hooks either, since glass is far too smooth to hook onto. The answer turned out to be hair. Look at the underside of a gecko's toe and you see rows of soft ridges. Look at a ridge under a microscope and each one is carpeted with millions of hairs called setae, thinner than a human hair. Look at the tip of one seta and it splits again into hundreds of even finer tips. All of that splitting is the point. It lets the gecko press an enormous amount of surface against the glass, close enough that the faint attraction between molecules takes over. Any two things pull on each other a little when they are almost touching. The pull is far too weak to notice at the size we live at, but a gecko has billions of contact points, and billions of tiny pulls add up to a lizard that does not fall. Best of all, it switches off. By changing the angle of its toes, a gecko peels each hair away and lifts its foot in milliseconds. Engineers have copied the trick to build climbing robots and tape that grips without any glue at all.

blocks.prompt: The Lizard That Tunes Its Own Color
blocks.text: For a long time the story went like this: a chameleon changes color to match its background, spreading pigment through its skin like ink through water. Half of that story is wrong, and the half that is right is far stranger than ink. Start with what chameleons actually do. A calm male panther chameleon sits green in the leaves. Show him a rival and within two minutes he blazes yellow and orange and white. That is not camouflage. That is an argument. Chameleons change color mostly to talk, to threaten a rival, to court a female, to signal surrender, and to control their temperature by going dark in the cool morning and pale in the midday heat. Blending in matters, but it is not the main job. Now the mechanism. Chameleon skin does contain pigment cells, yellow and red and brown ones, and those play a part. But underneath them sits a layer of cells called iridophores, and iridophores hold no pigment at all. Each one is packed with a neat three dimensional lattice of tiny crystals, arranged in rows like oranges stacked in a crate. Light bouncing off that lattice interferes with itself. Some wavelengths cancel out, one wavelength reflects back strongly, and that is the color you see. The color is not a dye. It is a structure, the same way a soap bubble or a beetle's shell makes color out of shape rather than paint. Here is the clever part, worked out by Swiss researchers in 2015. When the chameleon gets excited, it stretches the lattice. The crystals move slightly farther apart. Wider spacing reflects longer wavelengths, so blue slides toward yellow, and yellow slides toward orange and red. The chameleon is not painting itself. It is tuning itself, the way you tune a string by changing its tension. There is a second, deeper layer of larger crystals that reflects heat instead of visible light, which helps the animal survive strong sun. So a chameleon's skin is doing two jobs at once with no pigment involved: shouting at rivals, and managing the temperature of a small cold blooded animal in a hot place.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: More than 7,000 known species of lizard
Ectothermic: it takes its heat from the world
Runs on roughly a tenth of a mammal's food
Many carry a parietal eye on top of the skull
Komodo dragon: 10 feet, over 150 pounds
Zootoca vivipara lives above the Arctic Circle

blocks.prompt: The Solar Powered Animal
blocks.text: Ask most people what a lizard is and you get a list of features: scales, four legs, a long tail, a flicking tongue. That is a description, not an explanation. The thing that actually explains a lizard, the decision underneath every other part of its design, is that it does not pay to heat itself. You do. Roughly speaking, a mammal spends the large majority of everything it eats on one job: holding its body at a steady temperature, day and night, awake and asleep, in summer and in winter. That is why you are warm to the touch, and it is why you have to eat every single day. A lizard has opted out. It takes its heat from the world instead, from sunlight, from a rock that has been baking since noon, from warm sand. A reptile can run its whole body on something like a tenth of the food an equally sized mammal needs. That discount is enormous, and it buys a lizard two things. The first is the desert. A place with almost no food is a disaster for an animal with a furnace to feed, and a reasonable home for one that does not. Deserts are full of lizards for the same reason they are short on mammals. The second is patience. A Komodo dragon, the largest lizard alive, reaches ten feet long and can top one hundred and fifty pounds. It can swallow up to eighty percent of its body weight at one sitting and then go weeks without eating anything at all. No lion can live like that. Nothing is free, and the price of cheap heat is that the lizard does not control it. A cold lizard is a slow lizard. It cannot digest its breakfast, outrun a bird, or chase a mate until the sun has done its work, so the animal's day becomes a scheduling problem. Bask, warm up, hunt, overheat, retreat to shade, cool down, return. Watch a lizard for an hour and most of what you are watching is temperature management. Many lizards even carry a dedicated instrument for the job: a small pale scale on the top of the skull, called the parietal eye, with its own lens and its own retina. It cannot form a picture. It reads brightness, and it helps the animal track the sun, keep time, and know how long it has been out in the open. The bill comes due at the edges of the map. Sunlight is a reliable power source near the equator and a poor one near the poles, which is why lizard variety thins out as you travel north and collapses in the far north. The exceptions are instructive. One small lizard, Zootoca vivipara, lives above the Arctic Circle, and it manages this by refusing to lay eggs. Cold northern soil cannot incubate them, so the female carries her young inside her body and warms them with the only heat available: her own basking. Where the strategy stops working, evolution bends it rather than abandons it. It is tempting to read all of this as primitive, as though the lizard were a rough draft and the mammal a finished copy. That reading has the story backward. Warm blood is not an upgrade. It is an expensive option, one that buys speed and night work and cold climates, and it is paid for with a lifetime of relentless eating. Cold blood buys cheapness, patience, and the ability to live where almost nothing does, and it is paid for with a dependence on the weather. There are around six thousand species of mammal on Earth and more than seven thousand species of lizard. Neither strategy is winning. They are simply solving different problems with different budgets.
